decisions.reason: SOL keeps the meaning and voice; the past tense fits the narration.
“Were no exception” naturally preserves that Mutated Gates follow the same rule.
SOL keeps the threshold, alarm, and evacuation order without changing who receives it.
SOL preserves the Gate’s progression to a Monster Wave in a few dozen seconds; “form” is not relevant to this passage.
“Anything on record” preserves the unprecedented reading and the suspicion of measurement error.
SOL preserves the brief deliberation, the Kraken’s arrival, and the office being smashed first.
SOL drops the source’s image of disaster’s flames and the timing that it spread in an instant.
SOL keeps the Kraken’s power and the soldiers’ savage loyalty in natural prose.
SOL keeps both observed actions; the sentence break does not alter their meaning.
SOL preserves the Merman’s strange cry and the sudden silence at the crowded intersection.
The unfinished question remains interrupted, with a natural spoken reaction.
“The question went unfinished” preserves that the speaker could not complete it.
“In an instant” preserves the abruptness of the attack.
SOL omits that the trident pierced through the person’s body and flew straight through even the vehicle; BASE preserves both actions.
SOL states that the car exploded, while the source says vehicle fragments flew with an explosion; BASE preserves that distinction.
SOL keeps the alarms and phone warnings while naturally describing their arrival.
SOL keeps the noise breaking the silence.
SOL preserves what the people look at and their realization of the immediate danger.
SOL keeps the crowd’s immediate scattering and screams.
SOL preserves their focus on escape and survival, and that rules and laws no longer matter.
SOL keeps the interrupted, stammering plea and follows the required ellipsis convention.

SOL preserves Korea’s population-density claim and its timing after the Great Cataclysm.
SOL preserves Busan as the country’s second city and the intersection’s plunge into chaos.
SOL keeps the contrast that exceptions exist.
SOL keeps the figures moving against the fleeing crowd.

SOL keeps the command to attack the ones in front first.
SOL preserves their unfamiliarity and that a brief exchange sufficed.
SOL retains the one-to-ten-year experience range and their understanding of what to do.
SOL keeps the thought’s urgency and meaning in natural English.

SOL keeps the small number—around a dozen—at the intersection.
SOL preserves their lower Hunter standing and uncertain hope of buying time.
“Surround them” naturally conveys the order to form an encirclement.
SOL keeps their charge and abrupt stop as despair takes hold.

SOL retains the reveal that the first group was only the vanguard and the main force arrived.
SOL preserves the possibility that even this force is only a fraction of the whole.

SOL preserves the danger of facing a dozen and the near-impossibility for four low-to-mid-rank Hunters.
SOL retains the absolute impossibility without high-rank support and emphasizes it naturally.
SOL keeps the hesitant proposal to hold out until reinforcements arrive.
SOL specifies that the speaker was a man, but the Korean leaves the person making the suggestion unspecified.
SOL keeps the thousand-times-faster comparison and makes it a natural reply.
The shorter ellipsis preserves the pause before the curse.

SOL retains their families, will to live, and the duty and resolve that keep them from retreating.

SOL preserves the song, the singer’s appearance, and the hair covering her naked body.
SOL keeps the Siren’s bewitching voice, ruinous effect, and title as queen of the black sea.
“Haunting, powerful” preserves the voice’s intense and affecting quality as it fills the intersection.
SOL retains the fleeing people’s stop, the angel-like monster, and their rapt expressions.
“It did no good” preserves that their resistance did not improve the situation.
SOL keeps the blood slipping between clenched teeth and running down their chins.
SOL preserves the song’s invasive effect, weakening grips, and the approaching Mermen blurring from view.
The revised punctuation keeps the curse and its exasperated delivery.

SOL keeps the Hunter’s resignation and the interrupted moment before the song changes.
SOL preserves the cry and follows the required ellipsis convention.

SOL preserves the sea-colored blood, broken wings, and the Siren’s fall onto the asphalt.

SOL keeps the fixed-open eyes, dislodged crown, parted hair, and pointed object between her breasts.

SOL preserves the distant swarm, its ant-like movement, and the view through his mask.

SOL keeps his renewed offense and the fact he had briefly forgotten.

SOL retains the nearly thousand onlookers and their wide eyes.

SOL keeps his anger at the human making him endure the ordeal, without adding profanity beyond the source.
SOL preserves the deliberate assignment to the area with the most monsters and his physicalized resentment.

SOL preserves dodging the tentacle, stepping on empty air, and leaping higher.
“Time to finish this” preserves the decision to end the fight.
